did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with a plea for the LORD to reveal himself in unmistakable power: fire would blaze and make the waters boil, and the nations would tremble before him.
The LORD’s appearance is described as an event that affects nature itself: the mountains seem to melt in his presence.
The people emphasize that no one can know in advance all that the LORD will do; he will act on behalf of those who wait for him.
The verse presents the LORD as one who meets and helps those who gladly do what is right and remember his ways, but it immediately shifts to the people’s confession of sin.
The people describe their spiritual condition in stark terms: everyone has become defiled, and even their righteous deeds are like a filthy garment.
Sin is portrayed as a passing, sweeping force: the people wither like leaves, and their sins carry them away like the wind.
The people confess that no one calls on the LORD’s name or rouses himself to hold on to him, connecting this with the LORD’s hiding his face and the power of their sins.
One of the chapter’s central images is the potter and the clay: the LORD is the Father and the potter, while the people are the clay and the work of his hands.
The plea asks the LORD not to remain angry forever or remember sin indefinitely, and emphasizes: “Look, please— we are all your people.”
The destruction is described through images of desolation: the holy cities, Zion, and Jerusalem have become a wilderness and a wasteland, and the temple has been burned and reduced to ruins.
